text: Nobody at Meridian Outfitters was in the room for Lesson 29's lab. What they get instead is a document, and that document is what a CISO, an engineer, and possibly an auditor will act on months later. This lesson turns that lab's raw evidence into a real, professional penetration test report.

A brilliant finding written up sloppily gets argued with, deprioritized, or ignored, so the report is not paperwork bolted onto the real work -- it is the real work, delivered. The executive summary carries the business-risk framing in plain language for a reader who will never open the technical section, while each technical finding carries its own CVSS score, reproduction evidence, and a specific remediation.

Every finding is self-contained. The CVSS vector string shown alongside the 9.8 score -- network accessible, low complexity, no privileges required -- is the actual justification for calling this Critical instead of High. Evidence points to numbered exhibits like the Nmap scan and the sysinfo output instead of pasting raw terminal text into the narrative, and the remediation names a concrete action instead of a vague instruction to harden the system.

A list of findings without a schedule leaves the client guessing what to fix first. Ordering by severity, with a realistic timeframe attached to each one, turns the report into a project plan the client's team can actually execute against, starting with the Critical finding inside seven days.

Before any report goes out, a short checklist applies without exception: every finding is independently reproducible from the evidence given, no live credentials or unredacted sensitive data appear anywhere in the document, and the client's named technical contact gets a review pass before the executive summary is called final.

A report that can't survive that checklist isn't ready, no matter how good the underlying testing was. Lesson 31 picks up what happens when a report like this contains a finding the client really did not want to hear.
